Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 36, verse 80:

﴿The One who has made for you fire from the green tree, so that you kindle (your hearths) from it.﴾ That is, this simple, everyday observation itself confirms the aforementioned power of Allah. You people witness this every day, yet you do not grasp its reality. This green tree, full of the sap of water, when one part of it is rubbed against another, fire is produced from it, and this same tree then becomes fuel for that fire, despite its greenness and freshness. And through deep investigation, one finds that within the tree there is a treasure of natural heat, which it absorbs from the radiance of the sun and keeps gathered within itself, although it is filled with the sap of water. And from the friction of these trees fire is produced in the same way that fire is produced through the process of burning. Thus, through this true knowledge and understanding, this reality becomes even more clearly manifest: how fire emerges from a green tree. It was the Creator of the universe who placed these marvels within the trees, He who gave every thing its creation and then commanded it to fulfil the purposes for which it was created. Yes, it is our own heedlessness that we do not look at this creation from this viewpoint, and it does not guide us towards this Creator and Fashioner. If we look with open hearts and penetrating eyes, these secrets and mysteries are within our reach, and it is possible for us to understand them, to worship Allah, and to constantly praise and glorify Allah.

After this, the proofs of Allah's power are presented, and it is shown how simple this process of creation is, and how similarly easy it is for Allah to recreate people.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 36, verse 81:

اولیس الذی۔۔۔۔۔ الخلق العلیم (36: 81) "Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them? Yes! And He is the Knowing Creator."

The heavens, the earth and this vast universe are a wondrous creation. This earth on which we live contains millions upon millions of kinds and species of creatures, some so minute that we cannot even grasp their size, nor can we comprehend their reality, and of them we still know very little to this day. This earth is a small subordinate planet of the sun within a galaxy, and it is by the light and heat of that sun that we live. And our sun, which belongs to a galaxy, is one of some hundred million stars within that galaxy, from which our nearby world is formed. It is worth noting that there are several other galaxies in this universe, and many worlds like our nearby world. Astronomers can count up to about one hundred million galaxies so far, and they have done this counting with their limited-power telescopes, and they are waiting for more galaxies to be discovered when powerful observatories and telescopes capable of seeing very far are built. What is the distance between our galaxy and the nearest galaxy to it? It is a distance of seven hundred and fifty thousand light years. And what is the distance of one light year? That is 26 million miles. It is said that there was a great heap or mass of material, and these suns were formed by its scattering. This is Allah's vast universe, His vast Kursi, and our paltry and limited knowledge of it.

These suns, which cannot be counted, each have an orbit or heaven and sphere within which that sun moves, and within each of these suns are subordinate bodies, each with its own orbit. They revolve in those orbits around their own suns, just as our earth revolves around our sun. All these revolving billions of suns, moons and stars move at an extremely precise and determined speed, and never change their speed or orbit. They do not stop even for a moment. If that were to happen, all the masses of the universe that are now floating in these spaces would collide with one another, and this entire system would be thrown into disorder.

This space in which billions of celestial bodies are circling, and whose number is still unknown, is like tiny particles. Their image cannot be captured, nor can this circle be grasped by imagination. These are parts of a universe so vast and immense that the mind reels at the very thought of it. اولیس الذی۔۔۔۔ یخلق مثلھم (36: 81) "He who created the heavens and the earth is surely able to create the like of them." The creation of people is a minor matter, while this universe is very vast and great.

بلی وھو الخلق العلیم (36: 81) "Yes, indeed, He is the Knowing Creator." Allah created all these things, and He can create other things besides them, and without any hardship or effort. For Allah there is no difference between the creation of a small thing and a large one.

Verse 36:82: "Indeed, His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, 'Be,' and it is."

It is the same whether the thing is the heavens and the earth, a mosquito or a gnat, or an ant; all these things are alike before the command of Allah. Kun fa-yakun (Be, and it is).

Nothing is difficult or easy before Allah. For Allah, near and far are alike. There is only the directing of the will.

The moment the will is directed, the thing comes into being, whatever it may be. Allah explains it in this way so that people may grasp the works and actions of Allah; otherwise, the limited perceptive power of man finds it difficult even to comprehend things.

Now, in this Surah, a final blow is struck upon the strings of man's heart and vision. It is such a blow that it makes clear what the relationship between the Creator and the created is.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 36, verse 83:

﴿Pure is He in whose hand is the dominion (malakut) of all things, and to Him you shall be returned.﴾ (36:83)

The word malakut (dominion) expresses the importance and grandeur of the relationship between the Creator and the created. That is, every thing in this universe absolutely belongs to Allah, and Allah has complete possession and control over all that is owned within this universe. The second point is that all things must return to Allah. This is the final blow, and it is a most fitting warning for the extremely grand and awe-inspiring atmosphere of this surah. The subject of this surah is also extremely great and important, and the realities and proofs brought within it are likewise very great and awe-inspiring, and they are connected with and related to that great reality whose details and subject are given in this surah.
